sections.text:
After a painful quarrel, a letter goes back to Corinth, and it opens with comfort. God is “the Father of mercies and God of all comfort”, Paul writes, and he comforts us so that we can comfort others. This is the most personal of Paul's letters, written to explain himself and to rebuild trust.

He describes the ministry of reconciliation and says the good news is a treasure carried in clay vessels, so that the greatness of the power is God's and not ours. Pressed on every side, yet not crushed: it is the language of someone who has suffered and does not hide it.

Chapters 8 and 9 encourage generous giving for poor believers in Jerusalem. In the last chapters Paul answers rivals who mock his weakness. He tells how he begged the Lord three times about a thorn in the flesh, and reports the answer: God's power is made perfect in weakness.
Paul wrote from Macedonia around the year 55 or 56, some months after 1 Corinthians. The sharp change of tone at chapter 10 has led some scholars to think the book joins more than one letter.

What Paul's thorn in the flesh was (12:7) is unknown, though Paul says he begged the Lord three times about it and was not given what he asked; illness, opposition and temptation have all been suggested. The chapters on giving are widely used to teach generosity, and readers note that Paul appeals to grace and willingness and sets no fixed amount.

Paul opens with a blessing that comes from a hard place. “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort”. God comforts us in all our affliction so that we can comfort others.

Then he tells of a time in Asia that crushed him. They were weighed down beyond their power, and “we despaired even of life.” They felt they had received the sentence of death, so that they would trust not in themselves but in God who raises the dead. God delivered them, and Paul asks the Corinthians for their prayers.

He next defends a change of plans. He had meant to visit Corinth and had not, and some say he is fickle. He insists that his word is not yes and no, because God is faithful, and Jesus is God’s yes to all his promises. God has sealed believers and given the Spirit as a down payment. He stayed away to spare them. “We don’t control your faith, but are fellow workers with you for your joy.”

This letter is usually dated within a year or so after 1 Corinthians. The relationship between Paul and the church had been strained, and he writes with warmth and some pain. Some scholars think 2 Corinthians joins more than one letter, and others hold that it was written as one. The trouble in Asia mentioned in verse 8 is not described in detail here, and its exact nature is unknown. The Acts account of Ephesus is often linked to it. See Acts 19.

Paul makes a decision he explains with some feeling: he would not come to them again in sorrow. If he made them grieve, who would be left to cheer him? So he wrote a letter instead, and he tells them how it was written. “out of much affliction and anguish of heart I wrote to you with many tears”. He did not want to hurt them but to show how much he loves them.

There is an offender whom the church has punished, and Paul now asks them to turn. “you should rather forgive him and comfort him,” so that he is not swallowed up by grief. Paul himself forgives whomever they forgive.

He then tells of a restless trip to Troas, where a door was opened but he could not rest because he did not find Titus, and so he went on to Macedonia. Suddenly the mood changes to thanksgiving. God leads Paul in triumph and spreads the aroma of Christ, life to some and death to others. “Who is sufficient for these things?”

This chapter looks back on a painful stretch in the relationship between Paul and Corinth, including a severe letter he mentions and a person who had caused grief. The offender’s identity is not given. Many link him with the man of 1 Corinthians 5, while others think it was someone who had wronged Paul himself. Either way the chapter is a lesson in discipline that ends in forgiveness and restoration. The image of being led in triumph recalls a Roman parade and is read in different ways.

Some teachers carry letters of recommendation. Paul has no need of one, and he says why. “You are our letter, written in our hearts,” known and read by everyone, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on stone but on hearts of flesh. Any sufficiency, he says, comes from God, who made him a servant of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit. “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

Then he looks back to Moses. When the law was given on stone it came with such glory that the people could not look at his face, a glory that was fading. How much more glory belongs to the service of the Spirit. Moses put a veil over his face, and Paul says a veil still lies on the minds of those who read Moses without Christ. When someone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away. “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.” All of us, with unveiled face, are being changed from glory to glory.

Paul is a Jew speaking about his own Scriptures, and he is answering critics who question his authority. He compares his ministry with that of Moses, but he does not set the law against God, for the law came with glory. This chapter has sometimes been used to say that Jews were rejected or that the first covenant was bad, which is not what the text says. The old story of Moses’ veil is told in Exodus 34. Christians read “the letter kills” in several ways, and the debate continues.

Paul says that because he has this ministry, and because he has received mercy, he does not lose heart. He has renounced shameful, hidden ways and does not twist God’s word. If the Good News is veiled, it is veiled to those who are perishing, whose minds the god of this world has blinded. Paul preaches not himself but Christ Jesus as Lord. The God who once said light would shine out of darkness has shone in believers’ hearts.

Then comes an image people remember. “we have this treasure in clay vessels,” so that the power is clearly God’s and not theirs. He lists what that looks like. They are “pressed on every side, yet not crushed”, perplexed but not in despair, pursued but not forsaken, struck down but not destroyed. They carry the dying of Jesus so that his life may show in them.

He ends with hope. The outer person decays, but “our inward person is renewed day by day.” Present trouble is light and brief next to an eternal weight of glory, and the things unseen are the lasting ones.

Paul wrote this passage to a church that had doubted him, and here he tells of his own weakness without apology. The phrase “the god of this world” is understood by most readers to mean Satan, and some think it points more broadly to the powers that shape the age. The clay jars are the ordinary pottery of the time, and Paul’s point is that the contrast between the container and the contents is deliberate. Many have found these verses a comfort in hardship, and they should be read within Paul’s own account of suffering. See 2 Corinthians 11.

Paul asks his readers to picture a tent. A tent is a temporary thing, and one day it gets taken down. Yet he is sure that if the earthly tent is dissolved, God has something waiting: “a house not made with hands”. In the meantime he groans, he says, and not because he wants to be unclothed. He longs to be clothed, so that what is mortal is swallowed up by life. God has given the Spirit as a down payment.

From there Paul speaks of courage, of walking by faith and not by sight, and of the aim to please the Lord whether at home or away. He also says that everyone must be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ.

Then the chapter turns to the love of Christ and its result: anyone in Christ is a new creation. God was reconciling the world to himself, and Paul and his companions are ambassadors who plead, “be reconciled to God”.

Paul is writing to the church in Corinth, a church he helped found (see Acts 18), at a time when his own ministry is under question. Tradition and most scholars hold that Paul wrote this letter, usually dated to the middle of the first century. Verses 6 to 8 are read in different ways by Christians, who differ on what happens between death and the resurrection. Verse 10 is also read in different ways. For the hope of a new body see 1 Corinthians 15 and Romans 8.

Paul is pleading. He and his companions are working together with God, and they beg the Corinthians not to receive the grace of God in vain. He recalls a word from God about a time of favor and then says, “now is the acceptable time”.

Then comes a long list of what his service has cost: endurance, afflictions, beatings, imprisonments, riots, sleepless nights and hunger. Alongside it he sets a list of what his service has been made of: pureness, kindness, sincere love, the power of God. The chapter is full of turns that look like riddles. Unknown and yet well known. Dying and yet alive. “sorrowful yet always rejoicing”, poor and yet making many rich.

Then his voice softens. He says, “Our heart is enlarged.” Then he asks them to open their hearts too. The chapter ends with a warning about being unequally yoked with unbelievers, and a promise that God will be a Father to his people.

Paul writes to the Corinthian church, with whom his relationship was strained (see 2 Corinthians 2). The word about the acceptable time comes from Isaiah 49, and the promise at the end echoes Leviticus 26. Some scholars think the warning in verses 14 to 18 interrupts the flow and was placed here from elsewhere; others find that it fits. Christians differ on how widely the warning about being unequally yoked applies, whether to worship, business, friendship or marriage.

After a hard stretch, Paul lets his guard down. He and his companions had come into Macedonia and found no rest. “Fightings were outside. Fear was inside.” Then Titus arrived, and with him came comfort, because Titus brought word of how the Corinthians had received Paul's earlier letter: their longing, their mourning, their zeal.

Paul admits something tender. His letter had made them grieve, and for a moment he had regretted sending it. Now he does not regret it. The grief did not crush them. It led them to repentance, and he draws a line between two kinds of sorrow: “godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation”, while the sorrow of the world produces death.

He lists what that grief stirred up in them: earnest care, indignation, longing, zeal. The chapter ends in relief and joy. Paul is confident in the Corinthians, and Titus's spirit has been refreshed by them.

Paul is writing from Macedonia to the church at Corinth, shortly after Titus had returned to him with news. The painful letter he mentions is a matter of debate among scholars: some think it is lost, some identify it with 1 Corinthians, and some link it with chapters 10 to 13 of this letter. The first verse closes the promises of the previous chapter. For Paul's earlier anxiety see 2 Corinthians 2.

Paul starts with a story about other people's generosity. The churches of Macedonia were in a severe ordeal and in deep poverty, and yet they gave. They gave beyond their power, Paul says, begging for the chance to share in the service to the saints. They first gave themselves to the Lord, and then to Paul and his companions.

So Paul asks the Corinthians, who began this giving a year earlier, to finish it. He says plainly that this is not a command. It is a way of proving the sincerity of their love. His deepest reason is in verse 9: “though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor”. The gift is acceptable according to what a person has, not what they do not have, and he speaks of a fair balance between abundance and need, as in the old story of gathered manna.

The chapter ends with names. Titus, and two brothers well known to the churches, are sent so that the gift is handled openly and with honor.

Paul writes to Corinth about a collection for believers in need. Many scholars connect it with the collection for the poor in Jerusalem; see Galatians 2:10, 1 Corinthians 16 and Romans 15. The story of the manna that Paul cites comes from Exodus 16. The care taken over who carries the money shows how seriously Paul takes the trust of the churches. Chapter 9 continues the same subject.

Paul says he does not really need to write about this gift, because he knows how ready the Corinthians are. He has even boasted of them to the churches in Macedonia. But he is sending brothers ahead, so that the gift is ready, and so that it is given as a matter of generosity and not of greediness.

Then he reaches for the picture of a farmer. A person who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. Each one should give as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, “for God loves a cheerful giver”. Paul adds that God is able to make all grace abound, supplying seed to the sower and bread for food.

He also sees where such a gift goes. It meets the needs of the saints, and it overflows in thanksgiving to God. Those who receive it will pray for the givers. The chapter ends in a burst of gratitude for “his unspeakable gift”.

This is the second of two chapters on the collection that Paul has urged on the church at Corinth (see 2 Corinthians 8). The line in verse 9 comes from Psalm 112. Some preachers have read the sowing and reaping as a promise that giving will bring back money. In context Paul is speaking of a particular gift for believers in need, and of generosity and thanksgiving. Christians weigh the passage in different ways.

The tone changes. Paul has been warm and now he is on the defensive, and it begins with a quiet appeal to “the humility and gentleness of Christ”. He knows what is being said about him: that his letters are strong, but “his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised”. He answers that what he is in a letter, he is also in person.

He speaks about a kind of war. He says the “weapons of our warfare are not of the flesh”, and he names what they pull down: strongholds, imaginations, every high thing raised up against the knowledge of God. The battlefield is thoughts and arguments.

He refuses to compare himself with those who commend themselves. He keeps to the boundary God gave him, which reached as far as Corinth, and he hopes to carry the Good News beyond them. The chapter closes with a line that holds the whole argument: “he who boasts, let him boast in the Lord.”

Chapters 10 to 13 are sharper in tone than the earlier chapters of this letter. Many scholars think they are part of a separate letter, while others think Paul simply turns to face his critics. Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where some set themselves above him. The call to boast in the Lord echoes Jeremiah 9. The military language here is used of arguments and thoughts, not of swords.

Paul says he is about to play the fool. He is jealous over the Corinthians with a godly jealousy, as one who promised them to one husband, Christ, and he fears that their minds will be led astray, as the serpent deceived Eve. Others are preaching another Jesus, and he has preached God's Good News free of charge.

Then, reluctantly, he boasts, because others boast. Are they Hebrews? So is he. Servants of Christ? He is more so, and he lists what it has cost him: prisons, beatings with rods, a stoning, three shipwrecks, a night and a day in the deep, and dangers from rivers, robbers, cities and false brothers. Under it all lies something else: “anxiety for all the assemblies”. He asks, “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”

The chapter ends with a story that is almost comic: “I was let down in a basket through a window by the wall”.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, where rival teachers had been boasting of their credentials. He mentions five times receiving forty stripes minus one from the Jews. Paul himself is a Jew, as he says in verse 22, and the text speaks of his own experience, not of a people. The text has been misused against Jewish people. For the escape from Damascus see Acts 9. The limit on forty stripes comes from Deuteronomy 25.

Paul speaks, with great reluctance, of something he has never told. He knows a man in Christ who was caught up into the third heaven fourteen years ago. Whether in the body or out of it, he does not know. The man heard unspeakable words that may not be repeated.

Then he turns to something much harder to boast about. Because of the greatness of the revelations, “a thorn in the flesh was given to me”. He begged the Lord three times that it would leave him. The answer he received is the heart of the chapter: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” So he will gladly boast in his weaknesses, and he can say, “when I am weak, then am I strong”.

The last part is more personal again. Paul says he will not burden the Corinthians, that he seeks them and not their possessions, and that he fears what he will find when he comes.

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, defending his ministry against rival teachers. Many readers take the man caught up to heaven to be Paul himself, because of verses 5 to 7. The text does not say what the thorn was. Readings include an illness, opposition, or a lasting struggle, and Christians differ. The chapter gives no medical advice. Compare 2 Corinthians 11 and 1 Corinthians 2:3.

This is the last chapter, and Paul is ready to come a third time. He recalls the rule that every word is established by two or three witnesses, and he warns those who have sinned that he will not spare them if he has to come again. The Corinthians want proof that Christ speaks in him. He points them to Christ himself: “he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God.” Paul and his companions are weak in him too, and will live with him by the same power.

Then he turns the test around. “Examine your own selves, whether you are in the faith.” He prays that they do no evil, and says that his own authority was given to build up, not to tear down.

The letter closes with a call to rejoice, to live in peace, and with a blessing: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, God’s love, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.”

Paul writes to the church at Corinth, near the end of a letter in which he has defended his ministry. The rule of two or three witnesses comes from Deuteronomy 19. Verse 14 names the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit together, and Christians have long used this blessing in worship. Paul speaks here of discipline when he visits, and says its purpose is to build up. He mentions a third visit; compare 2 Corinthians 12.
